title: Winding Resistance Test: 7 Proven Steps for Accurate Results
text:
Motors & Drives

 Winding Resistance Test: 7 Proven Steps for Accurate Results

 A loose lug, a cracked strand or a few shorted turns can hide inside a motor that still passes its insulation test. Measuring the DC resistance of each winding accurately, and comparing the phases, exposes these faults before they burn the machine.

 
 4 Wire Kelvin 
 Micro Ohmmeter 
 Unbalance Percent 
 Temperature Correction 
 




 A winding resistance test measures the small DC resistance of motor and transformer windings to find loose connections, open strands and shorted turns. Done with the right instrument and a temperature correction, it gives a reliable health check in minutes.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a winding resistance test is done on motors and transformers, why the 4 wire method matters, how to calculate unbalance and how to correct readings for temperature.


 
 
 
 What Is a Winding Resistance Test?


 A winding resistance test is the measurement of the DC resistance of each winding of a motor, generator or transformer, followed by a comparison between phases and with earlier or factory values. It checks the copper path itself, unlike an insulation resistance test , which checks the insulation around it.


 The values are small, often below 1 Ω for large machines, so a normal multimeter is not accurate enough. The test follows Ohm law , with a known DC current passed through the winding and the voltage drop measured across it.

 What the Test Can Reveal


 Electrom Instruments explains that resistance measurements can find resistive connections inside or outside the machine, partial breaks in multi strand coils, open or shorted coils and wrong wire gauges. Some of these faults are not always visible to a surge test alone.


 
 High Resistance Joint
 One phase reads higher because of a loose lug, corroded terminal or poor brazed joint.
 Best for: terminal box and lead connections
 Hot Spot Risk 

 Open or Broken Strand
 Resistance rises when some parallel strands or a parallel path break.
 Best for: old or vibrating motors
 Hidden Fault 

 Shorted Turns
 One phase reads lower because turns are bypassed through damaged insulation.
 Best for: after overheating or a surge
 Burnout Risk 




 The relative balance between phases matters more than the absolute value. In a healthy induction motor , all three phases are wound identically, so their resistances should be almost equal.


 Do You Know?
 Copper has a temperature coefficient of about 0.0039 per °C, according to Electrom Instruments. A 10 °C change in winding temperature therefore changes the reading by roughly 4 percent.



 Why the 4 Wire Kelvin Method Is Used


 In a 2 wire winding resistance test, the leads and clamp contacts add their own resistance, which can be as large as the winding itself. The 4 wire or Kelvin method uses one pair of leads to inject current and a separate pair to sense voltage right at the terminals.


 Almost no current flows in the sense leads, so their resistance causes no error. The same idea is used in 2 wire, 3 wire and 4 wire RTD circuits, where lead resistance would spoil a temperature reading.


 The Megger guide to low resistance testing states that the four wire method eliminates errors due to lead and contact resistances. It calls it the most accurate method for circuits below 10 Ω.

 Quick Tip
 Place the voltage sense clips inside the current clips, closest to the winding. That way the contact resistance of the current clamps stays outside the measured section.



 Instruments for the Measurement


 For a winding resistance test, a micro ohmmeter or a dedicated meter is used, since both can supply a steady DC current and resolve microohms. Older workshops used a Kelvin double bridge, a relative of the Wheatstone bridge , and some still keep one for reference.


 DV Power recommends that the test current should not exceed 10 percent of the nominal winding current, to avoid heating the winding during the test. Its RMO50M model supplies 5 mA to 50 A DC and measures from 0.1 µΩ to 1000 Ω.


 Electrom Instruments states that its iTIG tester uses 4 wire Kelvin clamps and measures from a few microohms to 2 kΩ. Choose a range where the reading has at least four significant digits.


 7 Steps to Perform a Winding Resistance Test


 
 1
 Isolate and Lock
 Switch off, lock out and prove the motor dead at the terminals.


 2
 Disconnect Cables
 Remove supply cables and links so only the winding is measured.


 3
 Record Temperature
 Note winding or ambient temperature after the motor has cooled.


 4
 Connect 4 Wire Leads
 Current and sense clips on clean terminals, sense clips inside.


 5
 Inject and Wait
 Apply DC current and wait until the reading is stable.


 6
 Measure All Phases
 Record each phase or line pair with the same current.


 7
 Discharge and Calculate
 Let the meter discharge, then correct and compare readings.





 Always apply lockout tagout before touching the terminals, and remember that a large motor can also generate voltage if its shaft is turned by the load. Clean the terminal studs, because paint or oxide adds contact resistance.


 Take the reading only after it settles, since the winding inductance delays the current rise. On a large motor this takes a few seconds, while a big transformer may need minutes.
